![The Cheapest Ladder Is Also the Shortest](./cover.png)

Think about what each school subject quietly billed your parents. Chemistry
needed a lab. Music needed an instrument, and someone to drive you to the
lesson. Essays rewarded a childhood of being read to — years of it, paid for
long before you sat down to write one. Set against that, mathematics asks for a
pencil, paper, and maybe one book.

Mathematics has always been the cheap subject. It is the one arena where a kid
with no cultural inheritance isn't already behind on arrival.

## Self-verification is what it really offers

The low price is the obvious half, and the half that gets quoted. The other half
is that maths is self-verifying: you can know you are right without an adult's
approval. Where there is no adult at home who can judge the work, that is the
difference between doing it and not doing it at all.

It goes further than not having a tutor. Consider what an unstable home actually
does to a child. The rules move without notice. The same behaviour draws praise
on Monday and trouble on Tuesday. No adult's account of what happened can be
relied on, including accounts of things the child watched happen. A proof does
not behave that way. It is the same on Tuesday as it was on Monday, nobody's
mood alters it, nobody can talk you out of it, and once you have it, it is yours
and cannot be withdrawn.

That is an enormous thing to offer a child who has very little else that holds
still. I think it explains more of the funnel than the pencil does. Maths isn't
only the subject a poor kid can afford — it is the subject that behaves.

## Talent from poor households gets funnelled into maths

No entry cost, no gatekeeper on correctness, and a kind of certainty that is
scarce elsewhere: put those together and you get what you would expect. I grew
up poor in London and have since spent time in Mexico City, Guadalajara,
Guatemala City, Bogotá and Manila, and the pattern repeats in all of them. I
have no numbers for this. It is what I have watched happen, in six cities, to
people I knew.

What I don't think gets said is that the ladder is shorter than it looks.

## Cheap to enter, expensive to exhaust

The entry price is a pencil. The exit price is a decade of low income after
school, plus the network to convert credentials into money. Poor kids are
recruited on the first price and discover the second at twenty-two.

The outcomes are respectable and stable — teaching, statistics, actuarial work —
and well below what the same ability would have earned elsewhere with a family
behind it. Nobody lied about any of this. The subject keeps its promise. The
second price was simply never quoted, and the people best placed to quote it are
the ones who never had to pay it.

## The way off the ladder is a browser tab

There is now an exit partway up, and it is very nearly free. Every browser has a
JavaScript console sitting inside it. A bright fifteen-year-old who took the
maths route because maths was what they could afford can open that console and
be running code within the minute — no licence, no install, no permission,
nobody to ask. Computational work pays what mathematics does not. The pivot is
real, it is available, and it does not require anybody's blessing. It is the
same trick maths pulled: cheap, and checkable without an adult.

Its price is not the machine, or not only the machine.

## What it bills is the room you are standing in

To use a computer the way that pivot needs, you need a desk. A chair. A socket
that works and power that stays on. Two hours where nobody else needs the table,
and quiet enough to hold a half-built thing in your head across an interruption.
A shared phone is not a substitute — you cannot sit at a phone for an evening,
and everything that makes it convenient makes it hopeless for building.

A pencil bills none of this. That is the whole point of a pencil. It works on a
bus, on a floor, in a room with four other people in it, in ten-minute pieces
between other obligations. Of everything in this essay it is the only tool that
is indifferent to the conditions around it.

Which produces the cruel part. The children the self-verification argument
catches — the ones drawn to maths precisely because home is unpredictable — are
the same children least likely to have the desk, the quiet and the uninterrupted
evening that the pivot demands. The trait that routed them into maths is
correlated with the conditions that keep them there.

So the new ladder pays better than the old one and is harder to reach. The sorting
no longer happens where anyone is looking — not at admissions, not at the
scholarship, not at the exam — but years earlier, in whether the house had a
quiet corner and a working socket. That is not a thing funders measure, and I am
not confident it is a thing they would know how to fix.

The cheapest ladder was cheap because it asked nothing of the room you were
standing in. The new one asks for the room.
